Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 54 min read (10722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~54 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Molecular and morphological evidence increasingly supports the view that most East Asian Middle to Late Pleistocene archaic Homo belong to Denisovans1, yet the presence of other contemporaneous lineages has remained unclear.
  • It has been revealed that the taxonomic classification of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene and early Late Pleistocene hominins has been a subject of intense debate.
  • However, morphological heterogeneity persists among these hominins, for instance, cranial capacities of approximately 1,700–1,800 ml and a Neanderthal-like temporal labyrinth configuration and/or the presence of a suprainiac fossa in Xuchang and Xujiayao, and a round orbit in Maba10,11,12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Molecular and morphological evidence increasingly supports the view that most East Asian Middle to Late Pleistocene archaic Homo belong to Denisovans1, yet the presence of other contemporaneous lineages has remained unclear. Here we report a set of newly discovered hominin fossils (4 isolated teeth; more than 100.8 thousand years ago and 104.5–42.6 thousand years ago, respectively) from 2 cave sites (Chuanshandong and Longchuandong) in Guangxi, southern China. Integrated morphological and palaeoproteomic analyses reveal substantial phenotypic and molecular diversity consistent with at least two distinct lineages. One lineage (Longchuandong) is assigned to a Denisovan-affinity population, owing to its extreme similarity to Altai Denisovans with respect to dental morphology and single amino acid polymorphisms that match those of Denisovans from Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Altai. The other lineage, represented by the Chuanshandong hominin, is an unresolved archaic Homo, as it carries an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) shared with Homo antecessor and great apes and another variant (AMBN 253G) that is diagnostic of East Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus but lacks the Denisovan-associated AMBN 273V variant (it being highly probable that this is inherited from H. erectus). Dental morphology in this lineage exhibits a mosaic of plesiomorphic and derived traits but no clear Denisovan affinity. These findings indicate that diverse hominin populations may have inhabited subtropical China during the Middle and Late Pleistocene, including a Denisovan-affinity population and another unresolved archaic Homo.

It has been revealed that the taxonomic classification of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene and early Late Pleistocene hominins has been a subject of intense debate. These hominins are consistently characterized by plesiomorphic features, including a long and low neurocranium with a thick vault, a massive supraorbital torus, a sloping forehead and a robust mandible with a retreating symphysis, combined with derived traits such as an enlarged cranial capacity, a highly arched temporal squama, reduced prognathism and simplified dental morphology2,3,4,5. Phenotypic and molecular evidence has increasingly aligned these hominins with Denisovans2,6,7,8. For instance, the Harbin and Xujiayao crania, the Bianfu Cave radius, and the Xiahe and Penghu partial mandibles have been classified as Denisovan on the basis of palaeoproteomic and/or mitochondrial DNA analyses1,4,6,7,8,9. Phylogenetic studies based on trait matrices have linked Harbin Denisovans to Dali, Jinniushan, Hualongdong and Xiahe, suggesting a potentially broader distribution of Denisovans across mainland East Asia2.

However, morphological heterogeneity persists among these hominins, for instance, cranial capacities of approximately 1,700–1,800 ml and a Neanderthal-like temporal labyrinth configuration and/or the presence of a suprainiac fossa in Xuchang and Xujiayao, and a round orbit in Maba10,11,12. Such variations have led to the proposal of distinct species, that is, pre-modern Homo sapiens, Homo juluensis and a Neanderthal-related lineage13,14,15,16,17. Moreover, most specimens attributed to the Denisovan assemblage have originated from northern and central China, with few contemporaneous hominin fossils reported from southern China, particularly subtropical regions. Thus, it remains unclear whether the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo represent only Denisovans or multiple lineages adapted to diverse environments across a vast territory.

In a recent development, resolution of this question requires the discovery of more hominin fossils dating to the Denisovan period, especially from regions where such remains have not yet been reported. A comprehensive comparative study centred on such fossils should be conducted, incorporating a wide range of Eurasian Homo samples to establish a robust evolutionary framework for taxonomic identification. In addition to morphological comparisons, molecular analyses are essential for accurate taxonomic assignment. However, ancient DNA preservation is poor in the warm, humid conditions of southern China, particularly for late Middle Pleistocene specimens4,18,19. In such cases, palaeoproteomic analysis offers a vital complementary approach. This technology has been successfully applied to the identification of Denisovan specimens from diverse environments (including the Xiahe partial mandible4 and rib20 from the high-altitude Tibetan Plateau; the Penghu partial mandible6 from the Taiwan strait; the Bianfu Cave partial parietal bones, radius and teeth9 from southwest China; the Xujiayao cranium and mandible1 from north China; and the Harbin cranium7 from the plain of northeast China) and the phylogenetic placement of Homo antecessor (approximately 949–772 thousand years ago (ka)) and East Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus21,22.

A group of hominin fossils has been recovered from two sites in Nanning (Chuanshandong in Long’an County) and Liuzhou (Longchuandong in Luzhai County) within the karst terrain of Guangxi, a region renowned for its rich Pleistocene mammalian fossils, during surveys of late Middle Pleistocene cave deposits by our interdisciplinary team since 2016 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). These investigations spanned an area extending more than 500 km from Chongzuo City in the southwest to Guilin City in the northeast. The discovery of these new hominin remains in this area will be critical for clarification of the geographical distribution of Denisovans and assessment of whether multiple archaic Homo lineages existed in mainland East Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene.

Industry observers note that a, Geographical locations. b,c, Blueprint views of Chuanshandong in Long’an (b) and Longchuandong in Luzhai (c). d,e, Photograph (d) and schematic (e) showing stratigraphic deposition at Chuanshandong. Red stars in a indicate the locations of two cave sites in this study, while red stars in b, c and e indicate the locations where hominin teeth were recovered. Base map data in a from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com). Scale bars, 5 m (b), 10 m (c).

Here we present direct U-series dating results for hominin teeth from Chuanshandong and Longchuandong (more than 100.8 ka and 104.5–42.6 ka, respectively), the optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) ages of the hominin fossil-bearing layer (between 49.5 ± 2.6 ka and 34.2 ± 4.1 ka) and a biostratigraphic chronology based on the faunal assemblage (late Middle to early Late Pleistocene age, younger than 300 ka). To determine the taxonomic affinity of the hominins, we performed detailed morphological descriptions and comprehensive metric and non-metric comparisons with a broader range of Eurasian Homo specimens. In addition, we conducted palaeoproteomic analyses of hominin teeth and compared the results with published data from H. erectus, H. antecessor, Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens to further clarify the taxonomic affinity of these newly introduced hominins. The integration of these approaches will enhance our knowledge of the diversity of the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene hominins.

According to recent reports, chuanshandong lies in the karst terrain of Long’an County, Guangxi (Fig. 1). Two hominin teeth and associated abundant mammalian teeth were recovered from layer 3 of an approximately 1.2-m-thick consolidated deposit adhering to the cave walls of the western chamber entrance, the bottom deposit of which was eroded (Fig. 1, Supplementary Text 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). The sedimentary sequence consisted of the following six layers, from top to bottom: yellowish-brown sand (layer 1), consolidated brown calcareous-cemented sand (layer 2), greyish-brown sandy silt (layer 3), yellowish-brown brecciated sand (layer 4), brown gravel-bearing clayey silt (level 5) and yellowish-brown gravel-bearing silt (level 6). The two hominin teeth were separated from each other by approximately 5 cm vertically and 20 cm horizontally within layer 3. The deposit in layer 3 consisted of homogeneous, fine-grained particles without lamination, with grain-size and size distributions similar to those of modern soil near the cave entrance. They were all polymodal, mostly dominated by the clay fraction with very low proportions of particles larger than 63 μm (less than 8.4%) and relatively low percentages of coarse fraction (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1). This suggested that the deposit of layer 3 was derived from the modern soil outside and transported by low-energy, intermittent and short-term water activity. The hominin and mammal fossils from layer 3 were dominated by isolated teeth and may have been transported gradually into the inner cave by slope gravitation resulting from a depth gradient of approximately 5 m between the cave entrance and the burial location of the teeth. Therefore, the burial age of the fossils may substantially lag behind their true age.

In a recent development, longchuandong is situated in the karst landscape of Luzhai County, Guangxi (Fig. 1). Two isolated hominin teeth and numerous faunal remains were discovered in the brownish-yellow clay (Fig. 1, Supplementary Text 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). Given that most fossils from Longchuandong are isolated teeth, the fossils were highly likely to have been sorted and transported into the deep cave by water. No stone artefacts or other cultural relics were associated with hominin fossils at these two sites.

Industry observers note that to estimate the ages of these hominin teeth, we applied both laser-ablation-based and classic isotope-dilution-based U-series dating analyses to the hominin and associated mammalian teeth (Supplementary Text 2, Supplementary Figs. 3–5 and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). The lower right third premolar (P3) from Chuanshandong yielded laser ablation U-series ages ranging from 72.2 ± 1.4 ka to 63.8 ± 1.3 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 62.1 ± 0.3 ka. The left P3 yielded laser ablation U-series ages ranging from 109.2 ± 2.7 ka to 97.7 ± 4.6 ka and an isotope-dilution-based U-series age of 100.8 ± 0.2 ka. These two P3s could have originated from one individual, considering their similar morphology and degree of occlusal wear (minimum number of individuals = 1). The isotope-dilution-based U-series age of 100.8 ka thus provides a minimum age for the Chuanshandong. This age was also included in the range of the laser-ablation-based U-series ages of the associated mammal teeth (211.1–37.8 ka) (Supplementary Figs. 6–8 and Supplementary Table 4). However, the OSL ages of the hominin fossil-bearing layer in Chuanshandong ranged from 49.5 ± 2.6 ka to 34.2 ± 4.1 ka; that is, they were significantly younger than the U-series ages of the hominin teeth and most mammalian fossils, suggesting slow transportation or delayed burial of these materials (Supplementary Text 3, Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 5).

It has been revealed that the upper right second molar from Longchuandong (M2) yielded laser-ablation-based U-series ages of 46.9 ± 2.2 ka to 37.7 ± 2.0 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 42.6 ± 0.4 ka, whereas the lower right fourth premolar (P4) from the same layer returned laser ablation ages of 111.0 ± 3.6 ka to 96.7 ± 3.5 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 104.5 ± 0.4 ka. These ages fell within the range of the laser-ablation-based U-series ages of the associated mammal teeth (160.4–30.1 ka) (Supplementary Figs. 10 and 11 and Supplementary Table 6). Associated faunal remains from both sites represented a typical Ailuropoda-Stegodon fauna (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). The presence of Elephas maximus and Tapirus indicus, together with the relatively small tooth size of Ailuropoda in Chuanshandong and T. indicus in Longchuandong, all indicate a late Middle to Late Pleistocene age (younger than 300 ka). Despite the limitations of each dating method, the integration of U-series, OSL and biostratigraphic context supports a Middle and Late Pleistocene age for the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins.

We described the dental morphology of a pair of P3s from Chuanshandong and one P4 and one M2 from Longchuandong and compared them with a broad range of Homo specimens (including H. erectus, East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo, Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens) to determine their taxonomy (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 7–11). These materials occupied an intermediate morphological position between H. erectus and H. sapiens, characterized by a mosaic of dental traits and the absence of autapomorphic Neanderthal features. Nevertheless, the two assemblages exhibited distinct phenotypic profiles.

a,b, Longchuandong M2 (a) and Longchuandong P4 (b) from Luzhai. c,d, Chuanshandong left (c) and right (d) P3s from Long’an. The fossils and virtual reconstructions of the EDJ (shown in cyan) are displayed in the following order: occlusal, mesial and lingual views. B, buccal; M, mesial; D, distal. Scale bar, 5 mm.

In a recent development, the first phenotypic pattern was represented by the P4 and M2 of Longchuandong hominins. These individuals resembled the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo with respect to both M2 and P4 morphology and exhibited notable affinity to Denisova 4 from Denisova Cave (Altai) in terms of M2 characteristics (Figs. 2 and 3, Supplementary Text 4 and Supplementary Figs. 14–17). Their P4s shared an approximately symmetrical buccal and lingual contour (unlike the mesiobuccal protruding contour typical of H. erectus and distolingual protruding contour typical of Neanderthals) and non-tapering roots (distinct from the tapering roots of H. sapiens)3,23,24 (Supplementary Fig. 17). Their M2s had comparable hypocone size, similar enamel–dentine junction (EDJ) shape and a non-dendritic EDJ surface, distinct from the tall crown topography and the absence of a hypocone or only ridge-like hypocone of H. sapiens, and from the symmetrically trapezoidal EDJ viewed occlusally and dendritic EDJ surface of H. erectus23,25,26,27,28,29,30,31 (Fig. 3, Supplementary Fig. 15 and Supplementary Table 12). The Longchuandong M2 did not exhibit clear variation compared with Neanderthals, especially in diffeomorphic surface matching analyses of EDJ shape (the typicality probabilities of being classified as Neanderthals were 42.13% and 39.11% in the between-group principal component analysis and canonical variate analysis, respectively), although Neanderthals tend to be characterized by a more skewed M2 crown viewed occlusally and a higher occurrence of transverse crest (23.5% in early and late Neanderthals)28,32 (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 12). In particular, the Longchuandong M2 most closely resembled Denisova 4 from Denisova Cave (Altai) when all dental features analysed were considered, including the two-dimensional crown outline shape and three-dimensional EDJ shape, in addition to the crown size, relative hypocone size and degree of elevation of the crista obliqua, which overlap among different taxonomic groups to varying degrees33,34,35 (Supplementary Figs. 15, 18 and 19).

a,b, Bivariate plots of principal component 2 (PC2) against PC1 (a) and between-group principal component 2 (bgPC2) against bgPC1 (b) based on the diffeomorphic surface matching analysis of the EDJ of the Longchuandong M2 (Luzhai) compared with other samples. c,d, Bivariate plots of principal component 2 (PC2) against PC1 (c) and between-group principal component 2 (bgPC2) against bgPC1 (d) based on the diffeomorphic surface matching analysis of the EDJ of the two Chuanshandong P3s (Long’an) compared with other samples. The magnitude of displacement between the global mean shape and each extreme conformation is shown as a colour map from dark blue (contracted) to red (bulged).

It has been revealed that the second phenotype was represented by the paired P3s of the Chuanshandong hominin and did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member. These samples retained an erectus-like short EDJ that could be clearly distinguished from that of Neanderthals and H. sapiens and a complex root system with approximately constant root breadth from cervix to apex, which is normally found in H. erectus (for instance, the single Tomes’s root with bifurcated apex in Zhoukoudian and two-rooted pattern in Sangiran) but rarely occurs in Neanderthals or H. sapiens28,36,37,38,39 (Figs. 2 and 3, Supplementary Text 4, Supplementary Figs. 20–22 and Supplementary Table 13). However, the Chuanshandong P3s exhibited derived traits that were shared with other later Homo and distinct from those of H. erectus: reduced crown asymmetry, less pronounced distolingual protrusion, a lingually displaced polygon area, absent metaconid apex (probably sharper protoconid dentine horn) and a less crenulated mesial vertical groove on the buccal surface40,41. They were distinguishable from the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo from Panxian Dadong, which falls within the H. sapiens range, with a slightly asymmetrical crown and tall EDJ topography, despite a non-tapering root42 (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 22).

In a recent development, to provide molecular evidence for taxonomy and sex attribution, we conducted ancient protein extraction on three of the hominin samples: Longchuandong M2, Longchuandong P4 and Chuanshandong right P3. After searching against the Hominidae enamel database, we removed peptides that were detected in the extraction blank or attributed to contaminant proteins to control contamination from the experiment; this resulted in 2,894, 2,038 and 2,099 identified peptides for the three samples, respectively. The endogeneity of the proteome was supported by high deamidation rates of asparagine and glutamine, as well as relatively short peptide length caused by degradation (Fig. 4). We evaluated the replicate consistency by calculating the shared and specific peptide counts between two runs of liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) for each fraction from these teeth, as well as two fractions from Longchuandong P4 (Supplementary Table 14). Although more than 50% of total peptides were shared, indicating some replicate consistency, specific peptides from each run or fraction accounted for 40% or more in total; this demonstrated the necessity of conducting multiple runs or collecting multiple fractions to improve the coverage of recovered proteome. To avoid misassignment, we removed peptides matching multiple genes, and a typical enamel-specific proteome was retrieved from the three hominin samples (Supplementary Table 15). Abundant amelogenin, Y isoform (AMELY)-specific peptides indicated that all were from male individuals. We further inspected the phylogenetically informative single amino acid polymorphisms (SAPs) to determine their population assignments by validation with BLASTp, assessment of peptide depth across three software tools, evaluation of spectral quality and quantification of deamidation rates (Methods, Table 1, Supplementary Text 5, Supplementary Table 16, Supplementary Data 1 and 2 and Supplementary Figs. 23–28).

a,b, Deamidation patterns (a) and peptide length distributions (b) of three hominin samples compared with the published proteome6,21,46. The data analysis process for published archaic individuals was the same as that used for the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong samples, except that for Laos TNH2-1, H. antecessor (Atapuerca) and H. erectus (Dmanisi), we used an expanded database with the main dentine collagens (COL1A1, COL1A2 and COL2A1). In a, values were derived from 1,000 bootstrap replicates of sequence deamidation. Numbers of peptides containing N or Q with valid intensity are shown for each sample. In b, numbers of peptides are also indicated. In b, box plots represent the range of the data; box edges show the lower and upper quartiles, white squares in the boxes represent median values, and whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range, with black diamonds representing outliers beyond this range.

It has been revealed that both the Longchuandong M2 and P4 exhibited ameloblastin (AMBN) 273V (55 and 59 supporting peptides; Table 1), which is shared with East Asian Middle Pleistocene H. erectus, Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave, Denisova 25 and Denisova 3, and with some H. sapiens from Southeast Asia and Oceania with high levels of Denisovan introgression6,9,22,43,44,45. In phylogenetic analysis, the two Longchuandong samples were grouped with Denisova 3 with 100% support (Supplementary Text 6 and Supplementary Fig. 29). Given the age of the samples and the morphological similarity between the Longchuandong M2 and Denisova 4 from Altai Denisova Cave, the Longchuandong samples are likely to represent a Denisovan-affinity lineage in south China.

Unlike the two Longchuandong samples, Chuanshandong carried a SAP, AMBN 253G, supported by nine peptides (Table 1), among which seven peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) had a complete series of y- and b-ions surrounding the SAP. This SAP has been reported in three groups of late H. erectus from Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong22, but all other comparative specimens in Hominidae present AMBN 253A, including H. antecessor from Atapuerca21, H. erectus from Dmanisi21, Harbin7, Penghu6, Bianfu Cave9, TNH2-1 from Laos46, Denisova 3 (ref. 43), Denisova 25 (ref. 45), 9 Neanderthals47,48,49,50,51,52, Ust’-Ishim53, H. sapiens and non-human great apes. In addition, AMELY 179M, an ancestral variant that is shared with H. antecessor21 and non-human great apes but not with H. sapiens, Neanderthals or the Denisovan clade, was also identified in Chuanshandong with seven supporting peptides (Table 1); among these, two PSMs had two b-ions bracketing the SAP, and eight PSMs had one b-ion when the SAP was located at the amino terminus. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens (posterior probability: 100%; Supplementary Fig. 29). The integrated evidence indicates that Chuanshandong may belong to a lineage distinct from the Denisovan in mainland southern China.

The scarcity of hominin fossils from subtropical southern China during the Middle to Late Pleistocene transition has hampered our understanding of the geographical distribution of Denisovans and the potential existence of other Homo lineages in mainland East Asia. Here we report 4 isolated hominin teeth from Guangxi (Chuanshandong and Longchuandong), dated to at least 100.8 ka and 104.5–42.6 ka, respectively. These ages establish the specimens as contemporaries of northern Denisovans (approximately 300–45 ka)4,7,8,20,54,55 that provide key fossil evidence of non-sapiens Homo in subtropical regions adjacent to southeast Asia during this interval. Although both the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins exhibited a mosaic of plesiomorphic and derived traits, palaeoproteomic analysis revealed variations in AMBN 253 and 273, as well in as AMELY 179, which allowed phylogenetic placement of these samples. The results indicate that at least two non-sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China’s subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene.

Recent findings suggest that among these diverse populations, the Longchuandong materials provide compelling evidence for the presence of a Denisovan-affinity population in subtropical southern China. Compared with H. erectus and H. sapiens, the Longchuandong more closely resembled other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo, Altai Denisova 4 and Neanderthals with respect to M2 morphology but could be differentiated from Neanderthals by its P4 features. These two specimens carried the AMBN 273V variant found in Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Altai Denisovans, whereas Neanderthals and most H. sapiens carry the AMBN 273M variant6,7,9,43,44,47,48,49,53. These integrated morphological and molecular data together support the identification of Denisovan-affinity populations in subtropical southern China. In previous enamel proteomic studies, AMBN 273 was found to be polymorphic in Denisovans, with the M variant in Laos TNH2-1, M/V in Denisova 25 and Harbin, and V in Longchuandong, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Denisova 3 (refs. 6,9,22,43,45,46), indicating regional variation of molecular characteristics within this lineage. Taking the Longchuandong finding into account, there is evidence that Denisovans were distributed in Siberia, northern China, the Tibetan Plateau, the Taiwan Strait, subtropical southern China and tropical Laos, suggesting their possible adaptability to diverse environments, from cold and arid high-altitude plateaus to hot and humid low-altitude regions4,6,7,8,9,20,46,56,57. Neanderthals have not been discovered in regions with confirmed Denisovan distribution other than Siberia. Given their widely separated geographical regions, the morphological similarity between Longchuandong Denisovans and Neanderthals (for instance, with respect to M2) does not necessarily indicate hybridization. Instead, it may simply reflect the limited diagnostic value of certain anatomical features in distinguishing these two taxa. Unlike the similarity in M2 morphology, Denisovans and Neanderthals can be effectively differentiated by other dental traits, such as the crown shape of P4 and M1, the labial convexity and tuberculum dentale of I1, and other cranial and mandibular traits1.

Sources indicate that in contrast to Longchuandong, the remains from Chuanshandong were marked by an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) shared with H. antecessor and great apes and another variant (AMBN 253G) shared with East Asian Middle Pleistocene H. erectus but absent from contemporaneous Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens. In addition, Chuanshandong retained a plesiomorphic short crown and complex roots, differing notably from Neanderthals, H. sapiens and the Panxian Dadong (which is considered to be potentially Denisovan on the basis of broader dental comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo)42. Although Chuanshandong differed from East Asian H. erectus in having more progressive dental features and in the presence of AMBN 273M, the fact that they shared AMBN 253G implies that they may be related. The presence of an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) and an erectus-like variant (AMBN 253G) suggests that the Chuanshandong hominin belongs to a primitive Homo lineage that may have survived into the Late Pleistocene in a geographical refugium. Admixture among existing archaic Homo in southern China or gene flow from H. erectus are plausible explanations for the unique molecular and morphological attributes of Chuanshandong hominin.

The findings of this study show that the subtropical area in southern China may have hosted multiple populations of archaic Homo during the Middle and Late Pleistocene. In addition to the previously suggested Neanderthal-related hominin at Maba in the adjacent Guangdong Province16,17,58, we have now identified both a Denisovan-affinity hominin and another unresolved non-sapiens archaic Homo in this region. However, such phylogenetic inference based on the limited proteomic data is preliminary. More molecular data accumulated in the future, spanning broad geographical regions and time periods, and including ancient DNA from these archaic hominins, will provide us with a better understanding of the taxonomic value of specific proteomic mutations or variants and their variability between archaic and modern populations. Moreover, key diagnostic characteristics, especially trait combinations that significantly vary among different taxa, should be systematically screened from the relatively rich morphological dataset to define a lineage. Finally, it will be crucial to propose possible interpretations that can account for both morphological diversity and molecular variability, to further illustrate the framework of human evolution in East Asia.

A sliding calliper was used to measure the mesiodistal and buccolingual dimensions of the hominin teeth, with recordings taken to the nearest 0.1 mm. We applied the terminology and grading criteria of the Arizona State University Dental Anthropology System59, as well as the standards of Martinón-Torres et al.28, to describe and score crown characteristics, including the hypocone size, the crista obliqua, the transverse crest of the upper molar and the transverse crest of the lower premolar. Root structures of lower premolars were scored using Wood’s system60. The Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins were compared mainly with East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo or Denisovans, East Asian/Southeast Asian H. erectus, Homo heidelbergensis, early and late Neanderthals and H. sapiens.

To quantify the crown contour shape, cusp and fovea arrangement, and main occlusal groove orientation of the M2 and P3, we conducted two-dimensional geometric morphometric analyses on the basis of occlusal photographs of the teeth oriented in anatomical position following the procedure introduced in refs. 32,40. All specimens were digitally mirrored to the same antimeres as the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong specimens in Adobe Photoshop 12.0 when they were from the opposite side. Before semilandmark placement, the interproximal wear facet was digitally restored to its original state according to the extent of wear and the profile of the neighbouring contour.

For the P3 analysis, four landmarks were placed at the anterior fovea, posterior fovea, protoconid apex and metaconid apex. Forty equidistant semilandmarks were defined along the crown contour. For the M2, three landmarks were placed at the intersections of the buccal and central grooves with each other and with the crown contour. These landmarks delineated four distinct curves along the crown contour and in the occlusal grooves. Each of them was divided into different and equidistant segments, and the dividing points were designated as semilandmarks. In total, 3 landmarks and 36 semilandmarks were defined on the occlusal surface of M2.

According to recent reports, landmark and semilandmark coordinates were digitized using TpsDig2 v.2.12 (https://www.sbmorphometrics.org/soft-dataacq.html)61. Procrustes superimposition (minimizing Procrustes distances) was performed on the raw coordinates using the geomorph package (v.3.5)62. Principal component analysis was then conducted on the resulting shape variables. The ggplot package (v.4.0.3)63 was used to produce a scatter plot of principal component 1 against principal component 2 for visualization of morphological variation among different taxonomic groups.

The teeth from Chuanshandong and Longchuandong were scanned using the Phoenix V|tome|x M microfocus CT cabinet system at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. The scanning parameters were as follows: 160 kV, 120 μA, isotropic voxel size of 34.20 µm, 0.2-mm-thick copper filter. Microcomputed tomography data of Neanderthals from Krapina were downloaded from the NESPOS database64. Tomographic slices in TIFF format were imported into Mimics v.17.0 (Materialise, https://www.materialise.com) for segmentation of enamel and dentine and virtual reconstruction of the pulp cavity. The resulting EDJ was exported in STL format for subsequent shape analysis. The worn dentine horn apices of Longchuandong M2 and Chuanshandong P3s were restored by two observers independently following a geometric method validated in previous studies in Avizo v.9.2 (https://www.thermofisher.com/amira-avizo)65 (Supplementary Fig. 30).

The three-dimensional EDJ models were imported into Avizo 9.2, and all specimens were superimposed using the ‘Align Surface’ function. Following superimposition, the STL files were saved and converted into VTK format using ParaView v.5.6.0 (https://www.paraview.org/). The VTK files were then read into Deformetrica v.4.3 (https://gitlab.com/icm-institute/aramislab/deformetrica) for quantification of deformations among the EDJ surfaces, modelled as diffeomorphisms66. Control points and momenta encoding the deformation parameters were generated and imported into R v.4.1.0 (https://www.r-project.org/)67. Principal component analysis, between-group principal component analysis and canonical variate analysis were performed using the following packages: RToolsForDeformetrica v.0.1 (ref. 68), ade4 v.1.7-17 (ref. 69), Morpho v.2.8 (ref. 70), gtools v.3.9.5 (ref. 71) and freesurferformats v.0.1.15 (ref. 72). Two sets of EDJ, independently reconstructed by two authors, were also analysed, and the results were compared to provide an indication of the reliability of the virtual reconstructions of the worn dentine horns (Supplementary Fig. 31).

In a recent development, six samples were collected from the fossil-bearing layer of the Chuanshandong section, as well as two samples from the modern soil near the cave entrance, for grain-size analysis. Bulk samples were first treated with 30% hydrogen peroxide to remove organic matter, followed by 10% hydrochloric acid to remove carbonates. Subsequently, the samples were dispersed with 0.5 N sodium hexametaphosphate. Grain-size was measured using a Malvern Mastersizer 3000 particle analyser with an analytical precision of less than 1%.

High-resolution U-series in situ analysis using laser ablation system coupled with multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA–MC-ICP-MS) was conducted to directly date the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominin teeth. Laser ablation was performed using an NWRimageGEO high-energy laser ablation system (Elemental Scientific Lasers), and mass spectrometry was performed with a Neoma MC-ICP-MS system (Thermo Scientific). A high-precision MC-ICP-MS U-series dating method using solution nebulization after chromatographic separation was also applied to hominin teeth as an accuracy test. Integration of both procedures provided a minimum age for the hominins at Chuanshandong and Longchuandong. Laser-ablation-based U-series analyses were also conducted on freshly cut cross-sections of associated mammalian teeth recovered from the same stratigraphic layer within a 1-m radius of the hominin teeth (Chuanshandong). These analyses were carried out at Nanjing Normal University and the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, using the LA–MC-ICP-MS methods described in ref. 73 and the solution method described in ref. 74.

Industry observers note that the age of the hominin teeth from Chuanshandong was constrained by optical dating of the hominin fossil-bearing sediments. Three sediment samples were collected using stainless steel tubes (20 cm long, with a diameter of 5 cm) hammered horizontally into a freshly dug vertical stratigraphic section. The tubes were immediately sealed with aluminium foil, wrapped with black plastic bags and taped to prevent light exposure and moisture loss. Sediment from the light-exposed end of each tube was separated and used for dose rate measurements, and material from the middle was used for equivalent dose (De) measurements. Sample preparation followed standard procedures described previously75. Coarse-grained quartz (90 μm to 150 μm) was extracted for De measurements.

In a recent development, luminescence measurements were performed on a Risø Model DA-20 TL/OSL reader equipped with a 90Sr/90Y beta source for irradiation76 and an EMI 9235QA photomultiplier tube. Blue light-emitting diode stimulation (470 ± 30 nm) was used at 90% of 50 mW cm−2 full power, and 7.5 mm Hoya U-340 filters (transmission between 290 nm and 370 nm) were used for the quartz OSL measurements. The single-aliquot regenerative-dose protocol was used to determine the De (refs. 77,78) (Supplementary Table 17).

Recent findings suggest that the uranium, thorium and potassium concentrations of the three samples were measured by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry and used to calculate the environmental dose rate. In situ water content (moist mass/dry mass) was determined by weighing samples before and after drying and assigned an absolute uncertainty of ±5%. Elemental concentrations were converted into an effective dose rate using the revised dose rate conversion factors79 and water content attenuation factors80. The cosmic dose contribution was estimated on the basis of the burial depth of the sample, the thickness of the overlying cave roof (approximately 30 m), the zenith-angle dependence of cosmic rays, and the latitude, longitude and altitude of the site81. Final dose rates and deposition ages were calculated using DRAC82. Details of sample preparation, measurement and data analysis are provided in Supplementary Text 3.

Microinvasive acid etching was conducted on the tooth enamel for protein extraction, using an approach modified from a published protocol83. After cleaning with a disposable toothbrush, the tooth was wrapped with parafilm with the small etching region exposed. Then, the etching region was washed with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 30 s and rinsed with ultrapure water. We conducted an initial etch of 2 min by placing the etching region on to the 5% (v/v) hydrochloric acid solution in the cap of a 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tube. This etch solution was discarded. Then, a second etch of 15 min was performed twice in the cap of another microcentrifuge tube, and the etch solutions were combined. After desalting with C18 ZipTips (Thermo Fisher Scientific), the peptides were eluted into 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in 80% acetonitrile. The eluted solution was further vacuum-evaporated before being subjected to LC–MS/MS analysis.

A Neolithic human tooth from the Xiawanggang Site (approximately 5 ka) in Henan Province, China, was chosen as a positive control sample (referred to as ‘Xiawanggang’). The positive control sample and a blank extraction (negative control sample) were processed in the same batch as the hominin samples with the same protocol. All sample treatments were performed in the dedicated clean room for ancient protein analysis in the Molecular Paleontology Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. To evaluate the replicate consistency and improve the coverage of recovered proteome, we etched two spots on Longchuandong P4 and obtained two fractions. Two LC–MS/MS runs were conducted for each fraction from these teeth.

According to recent reports, the eluted peptides were analysed in data-dependent acquisition mode on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) interfaced with an Easy n-LC 1200 HPLC system (Thermo Scientific) at the Central Laboratory, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. A trap column (100 μm i.d. × 2 cm, C18) and analytical column (150 μm i.d. × 15 cm, C18) were used, both packed in-house with 3 μm reversed-phase silica (Reprosil-Pur C18 AQ, Dr. Maisch GmbH). Mobile phase A was 0.1% formic acid in water, and mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile. The peptides were separated using a 125-min linear gradient program (0–1 min, 1–9% B; 1–101 min, 9–28% B; 101–113 min, 28–42% B; 113–117 min, 42–99% B; 117–125 min, 99% B) at a flow rate of 350 nl min−1. For the mass spectrometry, full scans were measured with a m/z range from 350 to 1,500, a resolution of 60,000, an AGC target of 300% and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. The precursors were selected for higher-energy collisional dissociation fragmentation with an isolation window of 1.6 m/z and a dynamic exclusion of 60 s. MS2 scans were obtained with a resolution of 15,000, a normalized collision energy of 30%, an AGC target of 75% and a maximum injection time of 22 ms.

Industry observers note that all the raw data files from the hominin samples, as well as those from the positive and negative control samples, were searched using PEAKS Online (v.11.5)84, MaxQuant (v.2.6.0.0)85 and pFind (v.3.2.2)86. Multiple rounds of target database searching were supplemented with searching of a contaminant database used in a previous publication7.

It has been revealed that first, the data were searched against the entire human reference proteome downloaded from UniProt (proteome ID UP000005640, accessed on 20 May 2022) using PEAKS Online, including peptide de novo, PEAKS DB, PTM and SPIDER. The precursor ion mass tolerance and fragment ion mass tolerance were set to 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Unspecific digestion was chosen. Deamidation (NQ), oxidation (M), hydroxylation (P), phosphorylation (STY), pyro-Glu from E and pyro-Glu from Q were set as variable modifications, and a maximum of three modifications were allowed for each peptide. The peptide length was set from 6 to 45. A false discovery rate of 1% at the spectral level was used to filter the results. Proteins were accepted if at least two peptides were present. Main enamel proteins were identified in the hominin samples, whereas no dentine-related collagens were detected. This was not unexpected, because the acid etch approach can only extract proteins from the superficial enamel and cannot access deeper layers such as dentine. Thus, dentine collagens were excluded from further analysis.

A second round of database searching was conducted using three software tools against a custom-built database, referred to as the ‘Hominidae enamel database’ in this study. This database was composed of sequences for 12 main enamel proteins: amelogenin, X isoform (AMELX), AMELY, AMBN, enamelin (ENAM), amelotin (AMTN), odontogenic ameloblast-associated protein (ODAM), matrix metalloproteinase 20 (MMP20), kallikrein 4 (KLK4), tuftelin (TUFT1), collagen α1(XVII) chain (COL17A1), albumin (ALB) and α2-HS-glycoprotein (AHSG). Species were restricted to Hominidae, including archaic hominins such as Denisovans and Neanderthals. Protein sequences, including canonical and isoform sequences, were downloaded from UniProt and obtained from the translated Hominid Palaeoproteomic Reference Dataset available at Zenodo87. Previously published protein sequences from extinct archaic hominins (H. antecessor, H. erectus, Penghu)6,21,22, Paranthropus88 and Gigantopithecus89 were also incorporated. The parameters for data searching on PEAKS Online were the same as those used in the initial search against the entire human reference proteome. The parameters for MaxQuant and pFind were similar, with a few adjustments: for MaxQuant, phosphorylation (STY) was excluded from the variable modifications, the PSM and protein false discovery rates were set to 1% and 10%, respectively, and the ion tolerance and maximum number of modifications for each peptide were set to default values; and for pFind, hydroxylation (K) was also set as a variable modification, and open search was enabled. The possible mutations identified by PEAKS SPIDER and pFind open search were added to the original database for iterative data search and validation.

After removal of peptides detected in the negative control sample or assigned to contaminant proteins, we used the remaining peptides from each hominin and positive control sample to calculate deamidation profiles to support their endogeneity90.

It has been revealed that after excluding SAPs that were supported by a single peptide or indistinguishable owing to post-translational modifications7, we manually checked the variants within the Homo genus that met initial thresholds (PSM count ≥ 2, PSM ratio ≥ 10% and intensity ratio ≥ 10%) to confirm their reliability6,7,88. The criteria were as follows.

In a recent development, BLASTp: first, all the supporting peptides were submitted to BLASTp search against the NCBInr database. Peptides that also matched proteins from other genes or from some archaeal, bacterial or fungal species were removed from further evaluation and calculation.

Depth across different software: after BLAST filtration, variants were retained for further consideration only if each software tool retained at least two peptides.

It has been revealed that MS2 support: we manually inspected the MS2 spectra of all supporting PSMs to confirm the presence of y- and b-ions around the SAP. Two levels of criteria were applied: ‘MS2 support’ required at least one y- or b-ion linked to the SAP, whereas ‘strict MS2 support’ required at least two y-ions or two b-ions bracketing the SAP. An exception was made for terminal SAPs, for which a single associated ion was accepted for the strict classification. The number of peptides meeting each criterion was then calculated.

Deamidation rate: using peptides containing asparagine or glutamine residues, we calculated deamidation levels on the basis of spectral count and ion intensity. The number of PSMs and total count of covered N and Q sites were also recorded. An elevated deamidation rate in these peptides suggested an endogenous origin, which reinforced the reliability of the SAP identification.

Using these criteria, we evaluated eight positions across the three hominin samples (Supplementary Data 2) and confidently identified four of them. One of these was AMELY 59M, a male-specific SAP commonly used for sex identification83; details of the other three reliable SAPs are shown in Table 1.

Sources indicate that we combined the overlapping results from the three software tools and used them to generate consensus sequences for each protein from the three hominin samples with Biopython (v.1.83)91. For sites with more than two amino acid variants, we calculated the number of PSMs, the PSM ratio and the intensity ratio for each variant. In PEAKS Online and MaxQuant, a variant was considered to be reliable if it met all of the following thresholds: PSM count ≥ 2, PSM ratio ≥ 10% and intensity ratio ≥ 10% (ref. 7). In pFind, the intensity ratio was discarded. Confident heterozygous positions were identified as those for which multiple amino acid variants passed these filters. On the basis of the overlapping results from the three tools, no heterozygous positions were retained in the three hominin samples. Amino acid variants supported by a single peptide were excluded. The unreliable phylogenetically informative SAPs inspected above were also marked as ‘X’ in the consensus sequences. Finally, the consensus sequences of six proteins, AMELX, AMELY, AMBN, ENAM, COL17A1 and ALB, were reconstructed.

The comparative dataset contained four archaic individuals, five extant great ape species, a gibbon (Nomascus leucogenys) and a macaque (Macaca mulatta). The protein sequences of four archaic individuals were obtained from the Hominid Palaeoproteomic Reference Dataset87; these individuals comprised Denisova 3, Altai Neanderthal, Chagyrskaya 8 and Vindija33.19. Protein sequences for extant great apes and other primates were retrieved from UniProt and NCBI (Supplementary Table 18). The six proteins were aligned using MAFFT (v.7.490)92 and concatenated with R package phylotools (v.0.2.2; https://github.com/helixcn/phylotools), resulting in a dataset with a total length of 4,108 amino acid positions. We also detected 16.67%, 14.51% and 14.68% non-missing sites in Longchuandong M2, Longchuandong P4 and Chuanshandong P3, respectively. Leucines were converted into isoleucines, as these two amino acids are isobaric and were indistinguishable in the tandem mass spectrometry used in this study.

It has been revealed that we performed phylogenetic analysis on the aligned dataset using MrBayes (v.3.2.6)93. The best partitioning schemes and substitution models were chosen using PartitionFinder (v.2.1.1)94. Two Markov chain Monte Carlo runs were performed for 10,000,000 generations, with sampling every 5,000 generations. Convergence was evaluated using the average standard deviation of split frequencies and log likelihood values. Effective sample sizes were checked using TRACER (v.1.6)95. After 25% burn-in, effective sample size values for all parameters were greater than 200, indicating sufficient sampling. Then, a 50% majority-rule consensus tree was constructed, with clade frequencies representing posterior probabilities.

It has been revealed that the protein analyses of the hominin specimens were approved by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Guangxi Institute of Cultural Relics Protection and Archaeology. The researchers involved in the study are affiliated with these institutes.

Olympiacos duo Jota Silva and Lorenzo Pirola are looking forward to welcoming AC Milan to the Karaiskakis Stadium this evening.

Sources indicate that milan travel to the Greek capital hoping to get their Europa League campaign up and running. They have won just one of their opening four league phase fixtures, which was a 4-0 drubbing of RB Salzburg.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Defeats to Benfica, Bournemouth and Ferencvaros – all without scoring a single goal – have seen the Rossoneri slide into the bottom 12 positions in the table. With only 12 points up for grabs, they must start to put things right. By contrast, Olympiacos have won three of four, and sit sixth.

Industry observers note that jota Silva spoke to Gianluca Di Marzio about tonight’s game in Athens, admitting that the Rossoneri are a team that they respect despite their slow start in Europe. His words are via MilanNews.

What kind of game are you expecting?

According to recent reports, “It will be a great match, between two teams that usually play in the Champions League. Milan are a well-equipped opponent with an extraordinary history: they are a team we all respect. We are two historic and vital teams: they, like us, are having a good season.”.

They only have three points in the Europa League….

“They will certainly want to fight to advance to the next round of the European competition. They have players of excellent quality, including many internationals and many highly experienced players. Amorim is a fantastic coach and needs no introduction.”.

Meanwhile, defender Lorenzo Pirola spoke alongside his head coach Imanol Alguacil at a press conference on the eve of the game.

What’s your message for the fans, who will once again fill the stadium?

“As with every match, we promise to give it our all this time. We face a tough opponent. It’s another vital match, and we have a very significant evening ahead of us. We want to finish the game with a win and get the three points.”.

Having come through Inter’s youth academy, do you have any extra motivation for facing Milan?

“In any case, I spent four years at Inter, and it was a very wonderful and important experience. It’s a great experience to be able to play against Milan, but for me the most important thing is the three points from the win. That’s my goal.”.

Does the fact that this is a crucial match for Milan in terms of the league position provide additional motivation for Olympiacos to remain focused?

“It’s an crucial match for both Milan and Olympiacos, even though we have ten points. We’ll do everything we can to get the points we need to win and reach thirteen. We’ll give our all to achieve that.”.

Sources indicate that could this match also be a calling card for you for the Italian national team? Also, how much have Milan changed since you faced them with Inter?

“Considering that I’ve been here for almost three years and that my career is going well, I don’t see the match against Milan as a positive or negative opportunity for the national team.

“Milan are always a dangerous team and has a good squad. Anything can happen in a match, and as I’ve said before, we’ll do everything we can to win.”.

What do you expect from Milan in tomorrow’s match, and how do you see them competing for the title?

Industry observers note that “It will be a tough and intense match, with both teams pressing hard. I think it will be a very close game, and we’ll try to give our best. As for the league, everything is still open. We’re only at the start of the season, so I can’t give a precise assessment right now.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Minstermen, who ended their 10-year exile from the Football League last season, sit fifth ahead of Saturday's trip to Colchester United, raising hopes of successive promotions.

Lindsey is embracing that pressure at a club that have made no secret of their ambition to go back-to-back.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Industry observers note that "The only pressure I've got is from myself because I know what this group is capable of," mentioned the York boss. "I put pressure on myself to do well and believe that we're good enough to have a really good season.

Industry observers note that "I haven't got any pressure from anywhere else. It's a football club that want to get somewhere really quickly, which suits me as well.

Sources indicate that "I'm ambitious. I don't want to just make the numbers up and finish mid-table. It would be a bit of a waste of a season, even though that would be seen as success to a lot of people.

"It's our first season in the division for 10 years and I want to do really well.".

York have lost just four of their 16 games, bouncing back from consecutive defeats to claim their first win on the road at Rochdale before sharing the spoils with fellow promotion hopefuls Walsall.

City also have an FA Cup tie against Carlisle to look forward to for a place in the third round.

"I think we're in a really good position in the division," added Lindsey.

Industry observers note that "The football club hasn't been in this league for 10 years. To say we are where we are in the division and into the second round of the FA Cup, I see that as a massive positive.

"I'm over the moon with the start that we've had.".

Rather than making wholesale changes when he arrived in the summer, Lindsey has sought to build on the winning culture he inherited.

Maintaining the momentum generated in the National League was an crucial consideration as York made the step up to League Two, with the newly introduced manager recognising the value of what was already in place.

"Definitely," remarked Lindsey, whose side are just one point adrift of the automatic promotion places.

"The club before I turned up was a winning machine anyway, which is why I didn't change loads straight away. I didn't feel I had to because I thought there was a lot of good work done here.

"I just wanted to put my stamp on it, which I feel I've done, and the lads have taken on that information and executed it brilliantly.

According to recent reports, "It's a strange situation because when you come into a club as a manager, you're normally coming into a bit of a mess. But I wasn't; I was coming into a real structured team who were used to winning. I had to sit into that.

"My style isn't too dissimilar to what was happening before. There are little tweaks where I feel I've made us a little bit more robust for this division. Over the years of me being here, it'll be more my team.".

  • Looking to record back-to-back home victories for the first time this season, Moreirense welcome top-four hopefuls Santa Clara to Parque de Jogos Comendador Joaquim de Almeida Freitas on Saturday afternoon.
  • The hosts sit ninth in the Primeira Liga table, six points adrift of fifth-placed Arouca and seven behind the Azorean visitors, who occupy fourth position.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 26 Nov 2026 20:33.

Looking to record back-to-back home victories for the first time this season, Moreirense welcome top-four hopefuls Santa Clara to Parque de Jogos Comendador Joaquim de Almeida Freitas on Saturday afternoon.

The hosts sit ninth in the Primeira Liga table, six points adrift of fifth-placed Arouca and seven behind the Azorean visitors, who occupy fourth position.

Moreirense spent much of the previous campaign in contention for a European place but eventually finished seventh, and they are currently some way off the pace in the race for a top-five finish following an inconsistent start to this season.

Vasco Botelho da Costa's men have won just four of their opening 11 league fixtures (D2, L5), while struggling at both ends of the pitch, having scored 13 goals and conceded 18, the weakest defensive record among the current top-half sides.

The Moreira-based club enter this encounter on the back of a 1-0 defeat to Sporting Lisbon, which ended a two-match winning run following victories over Estoril Praia and Estrela Amadora.

Although losing by a single goal away to Sporting is hardly the most disappointing result, Da Costa will be concerned by a pattern that has seen his side suffer their last three defeats by the same 1-0 scoreline, including a Taca de Portugal exit at the hands of second-tier AVS.

Moreirense have also struggled for consistency on home soil this season, winning just two of their five league matches at Parque Moreira de Conegos (D1, L2), although a 2-1 victory over Estrela in their most recent outing at the venue gives them an opportunity to secure consecutive home wins for the first time since April and May.

Santa Clara, meanwhile, have enjoyed an impressive start to the Primeira Liga campaign, collecting 21 points from their opening 11 matches (W6, D3, L2), although Petit's side have recently seen the resilience that characterised their early-season performances begin to fade.

After going unbeaten in their first eight fixtures (W5, D3), the Azoreans have lost three of their last four competitive outings, beginning with a disappointing Taca de Portugal exit against lower-division Mafra before suffering a league defeat to Benfica.

Although they bounced back with a victory away to Maritimo, Santa Clara were beaten 2-1 by Gil Vicente in their most recent top-flight outing before playing out a 2-2 draw against Valladolid in a friendly on November 11.

Nevertheless, Petit's men remain among the hardest sides to break down in the division, having conceded just eight league goals, with only leaders Porto (five) boasting a better defensive record, while Santa Clara have scored twice as many at the other end.

Their away performances have been particularly impressive, with the Azoreans collecting 13 points from five league trips (W4, D1), giving them the third-best away record in this season's Primeira Liga behind Porto and Benfica.

However, the visitors have struggled in this fixture in recent times, going winless in their last four league meetings with Moreirense and losing three, including both encounters last season, which ended in 1-0 defeats.

Moreirense will welcome Tiago Andrade back into contention after the winger recovered from the muscle problem that ruled him out of the trip to Sporting.

Meanwhile, Alexandre Parsemain (leg) and Joao Veloso (muscle) remain doubts, while Francisco Domingues and Kiko Bondoso are still recovering from their respective muscle injuries and are expected to remain unavailable.

With Parsemain's availability uncertain, Leonardo Vonic could lead the line once again, although Yan Maranho is another option in that position.

Santa Clara have considerably greater selection problems, with first-choice centre-backs Pedro Pacheco and Emanuel Moreira both suspended following their disciplinary issues against Gil Vicente, with the former receiving a red card and the latter missing out through an accumulation of bookings.

Petit's defensive options are further limited by the potential absence of Guilherme Romao, who is sidelined with injury, though Pedro Ferreira could return this weekend if he is fully fit following a nose matter.

As a result, Ythallo could make his senior debut alongside Henrique Silva in central defence, although both have limited first-team experience, having featured predominantly at youth level and as a substitute, respectively.

Goncalo Paciencia returned from injury as a second-half substitute last time out and could lead the line here, potentially leaving Fernando to make way.

There is also good  news in goal,  with Lucas Franca having recovered from a muscle injury and expected to return to contention for the starting role.

Moreirense possible starting lineup:.

A Ferreira; Pinto, Kevyn Monteiro, Batista, A Martinez; N John, Liberato; Andrade, Mendonca, Landerson; Vonic.

Santa Clara possible starting lineup:.

Franca; Lucas Soares, Ythallo, H Silva, Fofana; Tavares, Borges, Vasconcelos; V Lopes, Paciencia, B Lucas.

Santa Clara have been considerably stronger away from home this season, but their defensive absences could prove costly against a Moreirense side that have won three of the last four meetings between the clubs.

Furthermore, the hosts have an opportunity to exploit an inexperienced centre-back pairing, although their own scoring problems and the visitors' impressive away record suggest neither side will have enough to claim all three points.

Latest Update: Doncaster Rovers 2 Huddersfield Town 3: 10-man Terriers emphatically end their barren league streak at bogey venue

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Certainly for the victor, if there happens to be one.
  • Do the business, put your feet up - well, sort of - with three points in the bag ahead of a long weekend and watch the rest of your divisional rivals sweat it out.
  • That was the hope for both Doncaster Rovers and Huddersfield Town in their differing third-tier missions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Certainly for the victor, if there happens to be one.

Do the business, put your feet up - well, sort of - with three points in the bag ahead of a long weekend and watch the rest of your divisional rivals sweat it out.

That was the hope for both Doncaster Rovers and Huddersfield Town in their differing third-tier missions.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The incentive for Rovers was moving out of the drop zone up to 18th, while Town’s ambition revolved around securing the win that would draw them level with leaders Stockport County at the right end of the table.

Huddersfield were the ones smiling as they finally made hay at league level at what had previously been a bogey ground.

The first ever visitors here back on Upcoming Year’s Day 2007 - the 20th anniversary is in a month’s time - Town had not so much as scored in any of their previous four visits at league level.

They emphatically put paid to that on a night when they played with a man light for around an hour. You didn’t really guess.

In a recent development, for the first 34 minutes, this game simply wasn’t a contest. There were 19 places between these two rivals ahead of kick-off and it revealed as Town cruised into a 2-0 lead, courtesy of Cameron Humphreys’ first goal of the campaign and a 15th strike of a goal-laden season for Joe Taylor before Bali Mumba’s Donny demons resurfaced.

In the league fixture here in February, a panicking handball saw him concede a penalty in the game-breaking moment.

In the present, he was the guilty party again - towards the same goal. He hauled down Jamie Sterry, who got on the wrong side of him following Robbie Gotts’ spotter’s badge of a pass.

Booked earlier for a sliding challenge he couldn’t complain about, Mumba was dismissed for a second yellow card—his second dismissal of the season.

Isaac Hutchinson sent the underemployed Matt Young the wrong way to make it 2-1 and out of nowhere, we had a game on.

But Town, not Rovers, grabbed the all-notable fourth goal.

Unconvincing at the back, the hosts erred for a third time and Ilias Bronkhurst fired in a soothing third.

Industry observers note that even without an extra player, it was Town who had the wit going forward as Rovers lacked penetration and quality. Given their defensive charity, it wasn’t a good mix and it's easy to see why they are where they are in the standings.

According to recent reports, A stoppage-time goal from home captain Owen Bailey revived Rovers, but it was not enough. Nowhere near.

Rovers, without the ineligible Alfie May under the terms of his loan, handed a first start to loanee James Collins, now finally over his long-term knee injury.

It was a psychologically important night for the veteran striker, who was injured almost exactly a year to the day on December 2, 2025 - ironically against Town. It was his last start.

Sources indicate that collins, who turns 36 on Tuesday, was afforded an early birthday present in the process. Sterry also returned to the Rovers’ starting line-up following illness. Brandon Hanlan dropped to the bench, with Tom Nixon absent.

Joe Low and Fletcher - lined up from the off for Town, coming in for Ibane Bowat and Bojan Radulovic.

Ahead of the game, Martin Drury had spoken about Rovers’ set-piece threat, with Low’s promotion seemingly something to do with that.

According to recent reports, A gulf in class saw Town stroll most of the first-half, aided by the meek defensive tendencies which Rovers had avoided five days earlier at Bradford City. It eventually changed.

The promotion of Ashley Fletcher, who had delivered a fine cameo in the Trophy game here in early autumn - looked the shrewdest of moves from Drury.

He teed up Humphreys for an easy low finish for Town’s opener on five minutes after Mumba’s cross caused initial consternation as Rovers prevaricated at the back terribly.

Town mixed play up impressively and afforded themselves plenty of control and possession.

In a recent development, last-ditch defending from ex-Terriers man Matty Pearson blocked Bronkhorst’s goalbound effort. A similarly alert block from Jack Senior repeated the trick to deny Low.

Town’s second was not long in coming on 21 minutes with Rovers again spooked by Fletcher, who indicated adept chest control and neat footballing skills to set up Taylor, who fired home a clinical low volley as Rovers again stood and watched.

A brief half-chant of 'We turn up, why don't you' arrived from disgruntled Rovers patrons in the Black Bank.

Mumba’s indiscretion changed the complexion of the night and Thomas spurned a chance to level before the break, planting a free header over.

Sources indicate that ahead of the resumption, Grant McCann threw on another attack-minded player in Hakeeb Adelakun. His side saw a lot of the ball in the opening part of the second period, but couldn’t conjure a significant chance against 10-man Town.

It was the visitors, who still possessed the killer instinct.

Sanches Fernandes rattled the crossbar and from the resultant corner, Rovers’ defensive deficiencies again re-surfaced.

The ball found Bronkhorst and after his initial effort was blocked, he rammed home a low drive in front of the ecstatic 1,905 Terriers supporters.

In a recent development, bailey ensured there was a nervy finale for the visitors, firing home from Adelakun's low cross. But it was Town's night, deservedly.

Industry observers note that doncaster Rovers: Simkin; Sterry, Grehan (Ayinde 70), Pearson, Senior, Thomas (Husband 84); Gotts, Bailey, Broadbent (Adelakun HT), Hutchinson (O’Reilly 65); J Collins (Hanlan 65). Substitutes unused: Clarke, Bryne. Huddersfield Town: Young; Balker, Low, Roughan; Bronkhorst, A Collins (Ledson 69), Humphreys, Mumba, Sanches Fernandes (Bowat 84), Taylor (Radulovic 84); Fletcher (Harness 55). Substitutes unused: Alnwick, Gooch, Ashia.

Attendance: 8,376 (1,905 Huddersfield Town supporters).

But Bali Mumba's second dismissal of the season - a second yellow card for hauling down Jamie Sterry on 34 minutes - gave Rovers hope with Isaac Hutchinson scoring from the resultant penalty.

But despite being a man light, the visitors produced an organised and controlled second half and managed to add a killer third just before the hour mark, courtesy of Ilias Bronkhorst.

Home captain Owen Bailey pulled one back in stoppage-time, but Town held out for a deserved triumph, their first ever in the league at this venue and following up their win in the Trophy at the Club Doncaster Sports Village at the start of September.

Drury said: “I thought we started the game really well and I really liked the way that the players showed real courage and belief early doors with the ball.

"I felt we competed really well in duels in moments where we had to be good because of the energy that Doncaster have and to score two goals early on, I felt we were in real control of the game at that point.

"We obviously then have the sending off.

In a recent development, "These things happen in football, so we have to respond from that. We're down to 10 men and it's about not just managing the game, but managing certain moments within the game.

"I thought the players were excellent, I thought they were outstanding.

"We had to defend some major moments towards the end of the game. We tried to get the subs right in terms of not just personnel, but actually size of people coming on in context to what the game might throw at us.

"Obviously, later on, you're expecting more set plays, more crosses into the box from the opponent, which is why we waited on that and got some more height on towards the end of the game.

Industry observers note that "I think the credit for tonight has to go solely to the players on the pitch. For everyone that started the game, everyone that came on and everyone that's been involved around it, I thought it was a real well-connected team effort tonight.".

On the dismissal of Mumba, who received his marching orders for the second time this term, he added: "I look at the last few games, Bali saved us two or three times in the last few games from those types of recovery runs.

According to recent reports, "These things happen in football. It's not something we're happy about, but it's not something that I'm going to start criticising. It's just something for us to work on and get better at.".

One significant downer on the night arrived with the news that midfielder Archie Collins come off in the second half with a hamstring injury.

McCann commented: "He doesn't look too good. He doesn't look too good.

Football video game EA Sports FC 27 to add AI-generated voice of iconic BBC commentator John Motson to latest game - three years after legend's death

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (498 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 10:33 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 04:18 EST, 26 November 2026.
  • The voice of the late BBC commentator John Motson will be featured on the EA Sports FC 27 video game through 'a mix of both his original audio and an AI-recreation'.
  • Motson, who died at the age of 77 in 2023, had served as the lead commentator on BBC's football coverage for decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 10:33 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 04:18 EST, 26 November 2026.

The voice of the late BBC commentator John Motson will be featured on the EA Sports FC 27 video game through 'a mix of both his original audio and an AI-recreation'.

Motson, who died at the age of 77 in 2023, had served as the lead commentator on BBC's football coverage for decades.

The legendary commentator had also lent his voice to Electronic Arts's FIFA series of games in the 1990s and 2000s.

EA has announced that it has worked with the blessing and in partnership with Motson's family to have him feature as an optional commentary selection in an enhancement of the latest edition of their EA Sports FC game.

The publisher stated its development studio 'has put Motson back into the commentary box with the aid of new AI-tools, bringing a mix of both his original audio and an AI-recreation trained by recordings of the man himself.'.

EA said its team worked with 'extensive care and respect to create a digital tribute to one of the game's greatest voices'.

The late BBC commentator John Motson will feature on the EA Sports FC 27 video game, through recordings and AI recreation.

Motson's family gave permission for the late commentator, who died in 2023, to feature in the game.

'My father adored being the voice of the game, and we are so grateful to the team at EA SPORTS FC for this touching tribute and preserving his memory in-game,' remarked Fred Motson, son of John Motson.

'His voice inspired millions of players across generations every time they picked up a controller, and now a whole upcoming set of fans will get to experience his legacy and commentary.'.

Motson's son also told the BBC his father would have 'absolutely' wanted to be involved in the game after his death.

The BBC reported that Motson's family were paid for the rights to use his likeness and to recreate his voice in the game.

EA added that AI had been the 'only way' for Motson's voice to feature, as there were no recordings of him talking about modern players.

While Motson's family gave EA's project their blessing, the use of AI to recreate voices has become an increasingly controversial topic.

In August, a group of 80 performers backed the Save Our Voices Now campaign, which is seeking to secure legal protection against technology which can clone a person's voice and make it say anything its operator chooses.

The campaign was founded by actor and voice artist Peter Caulfield and has been backed by stars including Hugh Bonneville, Nicola Coughlan and Matt Lucas.

Campaigners want Britain to follow the example set by Denmark, which has moved to give its citizens full legal control over AI-generated imitations of their face, body and voice.

The protections allow people to demand that any unauthorised content is removed and seek compensation for its misuse.

  • Coming off a three-week break from competitive action, Academico de Viseu and Alverca meet at Estadio do Fontelo on Saturday evening in what will be their first-ever encounter in Portugal's top flight.
  • The hosts occupy sixth place in the Primeira Liga table, eight points and five positions ahead of their visitors, who are four points above the relegation play-off spot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 26 Nov 2026 20:43, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 20:49.

Coming off a three-week break from competitive action, Academico de Viseu and Alverca meet at Estadio do Fontelo on Saturday evening in what will be their first-ever encounter in Portugal's top flight.

The hosts occupy sixth place in the Primeira Liga table, eight points and five positions ahead of their visitors, who are four points above the relegation play-off spot.

Academico de Viseu have made an encouraging return to the top flight after a 37-year absence, having collected six wins from their opening 11 league fixtures (D2, L3), scoring 15 times and conceding 13 at the other end.

Bruno Pinheiro's side, who failed to record a victory in any of their first four outings this term, enjoyed a particularly impressive spell between September 6 and November 1, winning six consecutive league matches, including a famous triumph away to Sporting Lisbon on October 25.

However, that winning run in the top flight came to an end last time out, when the Viseu club suffered a 1-0 defeat to Nacional in Funchal after conceding a late winner to Matchoi Djalo.

The result also means Academico have now alternated between defeats and victories across their last five matches in all competitions, including cup losses to lower-division Fatima in the Taca de Portugal and Primeira Liga champions Porto in the Taca da Liga.

Returning from a three-week hiatus, the Viseu club will be glad to be back at Fontelo, where they have won each of their last three matches, beating Vitoria de Guimaraes, Estoril Praia and Rio Ave by 2-1 scorelines after losing their opening two fixtures at the ground this term.

Like the hosts, Alverca also started the campaign slowly, failing to record a victory in any of their opening five fixtures, but enjoyed a three-match winning run between September 12 and October 12, beating Nacional, Rio Ave and Famalicao.

However, the Ribatejo club have slipped back into familiar struggles, having since gone winless in four matches across all competitions, starting with a Taca de Portugal elimination at the hands of second-tier Tondela before suffering narrow league defeats against Arouca and Benfica.

Sergio Ferreira's team then drew 1-1 with Casa Pia in their most recent outing, with Ian Luccas finding the net in the 66th minute to rescue a point, while the goal ended a three-match run without scoring.

Two wins from their last three league games on the road suggest Alverca have also held their own away from home, although they have been vulnerable when not at their best, losing three of their five away league outings this season.

There is also little to draw from history, given the Ribatejo club are without a victory in their previous three meetings with Academico, losing twice in that spell, although their most recent visit to Viseu ended in a 2-2 draw in February 2025 in Liga 2.

With no reported injury or suspension concerns, Academico head coach Pinheiro could retain a similar lineup to the one that featured against Nacional, with goalkeeper Ewerton shielded by the defensive quartet of Anthony Correia, Nikolaos Michelis, Robinho and Miguel Angel Brau.

Andre Clovis has scored five of the Viseu club's 15 league goals this season and also provided an assist, with the Brazilian expected to lead the line here.

Alverca could be without Rayan Lucas, who remains a doubt after suffering another setback with his left knee, although the midfielder has returned to integrated training.

Nabil Touaizi is also expected to miss out after suffering a relapse of a right-calf injury, while Bastien Meupiyou and Sabit Abdulai remain sidelined following knee surgery.

Meanwhile, goalkeeper Noah Raveyre is another absentee, with his return expected in early December.

Academico de Viseu possible starting lineup:.

Ewerton; Robinho, Correia, Michelis, Brau; L Silva, Messeguem; Guilherme, Kahraman, Mortimer; Clovis.

Alverca possible starting lineup:.

Mendes; Boyan, Gomez, James; Spencer, I Luccas, Gui, Chissumba; Chiquinho, Camara, Figueiredo.

Academico have struggled to find the net in recent weeks, but their overall league form and stronger position in the table make them worthy favourites against an Alverca side that have scored just once in their last four matches, so a home victory looks plausible.
